The test image shows a corn ear with husks pulled back, revealing kernels that appear mottled brown/tan with some pinkish discoloration. The kernels look damaged/rotted with possible white-to-pinkish mold. Top candidates: **Fusarium**, **Ear_rots_Gibberella**, **Ear_rots_Diplodia**.

Let me view reference images for these candidates.

The Gibberella reference showed unexpected dark/stalk images. The Diplodia reference shows bleached husks and grayish-brown kernel rot — matching the test image well. Let me check a couple more to be thorough.
Aspergillus shows olive-green mold, Trichoderma shows dark-green mold, Southern Corn Leaf Blight shows leaf lesions — none match. Let me do one more comparison.

**Analysis summary:**

**Test image observations:**
- Corn ear with husks pulled back, revealing rotted kernels
- Kernels are brownish/tan/grayish with a mottled, somewhat mummified appearance
- Some pinkish-reddish hue on certain kernels
- Husks are distinctly **bleached/dried** — a key diagnostic feature
- Overall ear looks lightweight and mummified

**Candidate elimination:**
- Aspergillus: No olive-green powdery mold — ruled out
- Trichoderma: No dark-green mold — ruled out
- Gibberella: Reference showed dark ear/stalk symptoms, no bright pink tip mold — poor match
- Fusarium: White-to-salmon cottony mold scattered on kernels — no visible cottony growth
- Southern Corn Leaf Blight: Leaf disease — not an ear
- Charcoal stalk rot / Goss wilt: Stalk/leaf diseases — not relevant

**Best match: Ear_rots_Diplodia**
- **Bleached husks** are the hallmark diagnostic feature of Diplodia — clearly visible
- Grayish-brown, mummified kernel discoloration matches advanced Diplodia infection
- The ear's mummified, lightweight, rotted appearance aligns with the description of "severely affected ears become lightweight and mummified"
- White mold at base (early stage) progresses to the grayish-brown discoloration seen here (late stage)
